So to explain the used terms more: Most train control systems operate under the assumption of a fixed block. The whole network is separated into blocks, there can always be only one train in a block. Each block is protected by a signal, there must always be a red signal separating one train from the next, and there are sensors that detect when a train drives in a block, when it drives out of a block and how many carriages (train integrity is important too).

For point based train control systems, operation of a train is only enforced at every signal (and on the way in approach at specific points), this means e.g. that a train does not run over a red signal, does not drive faster than the maximum speed, and has acknowledged speed limits.

For line based train control systems, that supervising happens continuously over the whole track.

Since the physical signals and sensors are expensive in installation and maintenance and railway capacity depends on the number of blocks on a track, line based train control systems support virtual blocks. This means that the signals and sensors are not physically there, but simulated by computers (on the train and signalbox). From the view of the point based train control that means multiple trains are in a single block, because it does not know about the virtual subblocks. When a train is running that only supports point based train control it can only use whole blocks, so the capacity is simply reduced, but it is still safe, because every physical block is also known in the line based control system.

When the line based train control system stops being in use, the fundamental constraint of the point based train control system is being violated: there are multiple trains that are in a single block, and hence not actually protected by a red signal in between. This means that you must ignore the signals until every train has crossed at least one physical signal.

(This is speculation:) It seems that that the operators assumed that there is still a safety system in place, that they can rely on. Hence they did no tell the trains to use manual operation, (which might also require driving by sight [max. 40km/h], but not necessarily, I don't know the proper procedure in Spain), but told them to fall back to the normal safety system. It's reported that some train drivers and dispatchers questioned that, but that can also be an translation error and instead them repeating what was said, as is proper safety procedure. But the point based train control system will show a green signal, even if there is actually a train in front, because it is in the same block as you, but the signal shows whether you are allowed to drive in the next block, not into the current, as you are already in the current block. This seemed to be what happened here, the second train saw the green signal thought they are back in the automatic safety system and accelerated to 200km/h, not knowing that there is still a train in front. The first train should have also started driving, but did not, due to an error in the train. In normal situations this should never cause an accident, but in this case the accident would not have occurred if that wouldn't have taken place, but that would have been simply by luck.

You can see the green signal in some of the pictures, which to me looks really weird (kinda like a both dead and alive corps), because I would expect to put all signals to red in the case of an accident. I would expect to do that, while you are calling the emergency number, but I do not know if that is the procedure in Spain. You also see in the pictures that the whole cluster traveled about a train length and that the last carriages of the first and the first of the second train are merged into one. This indicates a surprisingly high speed for the crash, above 100km/h. That fits the explanation of the second train not being able to see the first until directly up to a few 100 meters before.

There were actually more trains in that block, so it's pure luck, that there were "only" two trains involved in this accident. Also some claimed, that there was a curve directly before, so the second train couldn't see the first until directly up to the accident. This would not have prevented the accident, it would have just reduced the involved crash speed and hence reduced the number of dead people.

It's quite ironic, that the accident would have likely not happened in case of no safety system being present.

---

Actual classical collisions of two trains like in this case are quite rare, because that's like the first purpose of every train control system, which exist since the 1870s. The accident from January this year in Spain was also a collision, but because a train derailed, while another train passed it. This can't really be prevented by a current train control system, other then not allowing the derailment to happen in the first place. Derailment in carriages is actually not rare at all, but daily, it's like going slightly on the shoulders of the street with your car, but train derailments are.

The accident from Meerbusch-Osterath from 2017 is similar in that is was also a collision. The cause itself is not really similar. The normal train control also failed, so the trains need to be operated manually. For that it was still relied on the automatic train detection and labeling system, but that had a bug (and some operator error due to a bug, this is simplified) and showed the number of the second train, where the block of the first train was. So they allowed the second train to advance. They did have contact with the first train, because they noticed something was wrong, but that driver didn't properly speak German and also failed to look out of the window directly where a hectometer sign was, so he couldn't tell the dispatchers were he actually was. The dispatcher forgot to tell the driver of the second train to use drive by sight (40km/h), so he accelerated to full speed (120km/h). The accident only caused 40 injured people and no deaths, because the second driver saw the first train. The accident happened at night, in the dark and at a speed of 85km/h. Train dispatchers are supposed to keep track of the trains and the actions they do too, but since the automatic train detection and labeling works most of the time, it becomes easy to rely on it.

The accident from Fallersleben from 2002 is similar, because the original failure of LZB and fallback to PZB is the same. Hence there was also more than one train in one block. The signalbox software told the second train to advance to full speed and the first to stop. This would have caused a crash, but the train driver of the second train noticed, that couldn't be and notified the dispatcher who then told them to not proceed, hence the accident didn't happen. So to explain the used terms more: Most train control systems operate under the assumption of a fixed block. The whole network is separated into blocks, there can always be only one train in a block. Each block is protected by a signal, there must always be a red signal separating one train from the next, and there are sensors that detect when a train drives in a block, when it drives out of a block and how many carriages (train integrity is important too).

For point based train control systems, operation of a train is only enforced at every signal (and on the way in approach at specific points), this means e.g. that a train does not run over a red signal, does not drive faster than the maximum speed, and has acknowledged speed limits.

For line based train control systems, that supervising happens continuously over the whole track.

Since the physical signals and sensors are expensive in installation and maintenance and railway capacity depends on the number of blocks on a track, line based train control systems support virtual blocks. This means that the signals and sensors are not physically there, but simulated by computers (on the train and signalbox). From the view of the point based train control that means multiple trains are in a single block, because it does not know about the virtual subblocks. When a train is running that only supports point based train control it can only use whole blocks, so the capacity is simply reduced, but it is still safe, because every physical block is also known in the line based control system.

When the line based train control system stops being in use, the fundamental constraint of the point based train control system is being violated: there are multiple trains that are in a single block, and hence not actually protected by a red signal in between. This means that you must ignore the signals until every train has crossed at least one physical signal.

(This is speculation:) It seems that that the operators assumed that there is still a safety system in place, that they can rely on. Hence they did no tell the trains to use manual operation, (which might also require driving by sight [max. 40km/h], but not necessarily, I don't know the proper procedure in Spain), but told them to fall back to the normal safety system. It's reported that some train drivers and dispatchers questioned that, but that can also be an translation error and instead them repeating what was said, as is proper safety procedure. But the point based train control system will show a green signal, even if there is actually a train in front, because it is in the same block as you, but the signal shows whether you are allowed to drive in the next block, not into the current, as you are already in the current block. This seemed to be what happened here, the second train saw the green signal thought they are back in the automatic safety system and accelerated to 200km/h, not knowing that there is still a train in front. The first train should have also started driving, but did not, due to an error in the train. In normal situations this should never cause an accident, but in this case the accident would not have occurred if that wouldn't have taken place, but that would have been simply by luck.

You can see the green signal in some of the pictures, which to me looks really weird (kinda like a both dead and alive corps), because I would expect to put all signals to red in the case of an accident. I would expect to do that, while you are calling the emergency number, but I do not know if that is the procedure in Spain. You also see in the pictures that the whole cluster traveled about a train length and that the last carriages of the first and the first of the second train are merged into one. This indicates a surprisingly high speed for the crash, above 100km/h. That fits the explanation of the second train not being able to see the first until directly up to a few 100 meters before.

There were actually more trains in that block, so it's pure luck, that there were "only" two trains involved in this accident. Also some claimed, that there was a curve directly before, so the second train couldn't see the first until directly up to the accident. This would not have prevented the accident, it would have just reduced the involved crash speed and hence reduced the number of dead people.

It's quite ironic, that the accident would have likely not happened in case of no safety system being present.

---

Actual classical collisions of two trains like in this case are quite rare, because that's like the first purpose of every train control system, which exist since the 1870s. The accident from January this year in Spain was also a collision, but because a train derailed, while another train passed it. This can't really be prevented by a current train control system, other then not allowing the derailment to happen in the first place. Derailment in carriages is actually not rare at all, but daily, it's like going slightly on the shoulders of the street with your car, but train derailments are.

The accident from Meerbusch-Osterath from 2017 is similar in that is was also a collision. The cause itself is not really similar. The normal train control also failed, so the trains need to be operated manually. For that it was still relied on the automatic train detection and labeling system, but that had a bug (and some operator error due to a bug, this is simplified) and showed the number of the second train, where the block of the first train was. So they allowed the second train to advance. They did have contact with the first train, because they noticed something was wrong, but that driver didn't properly speak German and also failed to look out of the window directly where a hectometer sign was, so he couldn't tell the dispatchers were he actually was. The dispatcher forgot to tell the driver of the second train to use drive by sight (40km/h), so he accelerated to full speed (120km/h). The accident only caused 40 injured people and no deaths, because the second driver saw the first train. The accident happened at night, in the dark and at a speed of 85km/h. Train dispatchers are supposed to keep track of the trains and the actions they do too, but since the automatic train detection and labeling works most of the time, it becomes easy to rely on it.

The accident from Fallersleben from 2002 is similar, because the original failure of LZB and fallback to PZB is the same. Hence there was also more than one train in one block. The signalbox software told the second train to advance to full speed and the first to stop. This would have caused a crash, but the train driver of the second train noticed, that couldn't be and notified the dispatcher who then told them to not proceed, hence the accident didn't happen. This caused it to become mandatory to let the first train to drive again operate on sight [40 km/h].

I'm not naive enough to think that these companies don't already have some internal detection tools, but they clearly are not being used enough. Lately researching anything using agents has been a pain (especially if the query leads up to buying intent) - the sources quoted are often AI slop, which are then used to deterministically argue a point. On the first challenge to logic, the reply is usually an apology followed by a tangential search and agreement on the user argued point - sometimes even a hedge. There is a simple problem embedded at the center of this, that at least partially explains this degradation - AI generated text. There is now arguably more AI generated text on the web than human writings, and platforms that used to be very credible (attracting high quality technical writers) now seem to be full of AI generated slop (someone has to call them out). It's a pattern I'm sure most people are noticing under the hood - query -> beautiful prose -> suspect sources. You challenge the answer, and all of a sudden it's a wildly different conclusion. To me that just sounds unreliable, because you could potentially argue with it to generate any conclusion you want - doesn't sound like a reliable brainstorming partner anymore. Not to mention it's preference for believing structured AI prose output as high quality writing. Perhaps it is simply a byproduct of the baked in agreeability or "dooms-day" protections baked in to system prompts. This makes it even more important to have sources quoted by bots verified for authority and origin. The authority test is being easily faked by rampant SEO abuse on once reliable blogging platforms (I won't name them but you know who) - apparently one bot - sorry user - singing product praises is enough for chat to recommend that product, mind-boggling. And one biased - sorry tailored - article comparing a product to 5 competitors is enough to determine which is best. If this is not a crisis, idk what is.

The detection problem: Using conventional techniques like duplicate detection, repetition and similarity filters on AI generated content is a lost cause - there's enough probabilistic variance in them to generate millions of different copies.

One solution to the problem: Use an AI detector to adjust result ranks. By adjusting the ranking using AI generated labels, not only will engines prioritise genuine human writings - they also potentially refer to a wider range of opinions on a subject, improving diversity consulted in answers. I know it sounds like an over-simplification, and it probably is - but to me it does sound like a first step in the right direction.

Taken from https://t9xt.com/writings/why-google-microsoft-anthropic-and-openai-need-to-build-their-own-ai-detection-tools-before-it-i

At Researchly (https://www.researchly.at) we automate market and competitive analysis. We learned that on-the-fly web search through AI agents isn't reliable enough for consistent, in-depth work.

Existing data providers such as PitchBook or Crunchbase are either too expensive or lack the data we need: operational signals such as management changes or new partnerships, for DACH. Furthermore, search tools such as Exa tend to be probabilistic. What they return depends on the model and on SEO rankings, so two runs of the same query can give you two different answers.

So we built our own search layer: several providers (Exa, Linkup, Tavily, Parallel), allow/deny lists, source rankings (we once caught ourselves citing our own blog posts), and checks whether an empty result means "nothing there" or "out of budget".

It works, but: it's slow, expensive, non-deterministic & we kept redoing the same research for different clients (which makes it very un-economic).

So we started building the data layer itself. Step one was Firmendaten (300k companies from the Austrian register; shared here last week https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50142669).

Relational data like that is already a huge improvement, but what we really need is a graph, as people ask "W" questions: who does what with whom where and when. This is our first attempt at it.

For now, it just connects who partners with whom and company groups. (Tick "Beziehungen 2. Ebene" to see every partner and person)

It's small (a few dozen robotics companies) but you can already see how complex the graph gets & it serves as a good PoC for us.

We had wanted to build this for a long time, and it turned out to be far harder than we expected. One thing that sounds trivial but was particularly hard: finding the right website for a company.

You can buy that data. There are enrichment APIs that return a company's website. But even if they cover Austrian companies, how do you know which company they matched? There is no worldwide unique company identifier.

And if you do it yourself: how do you know that this website really belongs to this company? You have to validate every single match (e. g. through the imprint on a company's website in Austria).

There are quite a few more challenges involved, but we're happy with where this first, admittedly small, result has landed. Feedback very welcome – especially on which relationships would make a graph like this useful for you.

Feedback welcome!

Yes, and humans evolved in an environment of resource scarcity. Literally every instinct we have, including addiction and every psychological condition we categorize as mental illness, is tuned to that.

> But aren't there additional systems that can detect that a block is obstructed (e.g. also by left behind carriages that got disconnected) like the electrical track circuit (Gleisstromkreis)?

That's not an additional system, that is the PZB (or here ASFA).

> Or wouldn't that have helped because we're back again to the issue that with the downgrade from LZB to PZB we lost the virtual blocks, and both trains are now occupying the same, longer, non-virtual block?

Yes.

> But they have no indication that there is a second train (Iryo) in front, occupying the same block.

We don't know what they missed, and speculating on that is quite pointless, if we want to have that discussion, we need to wait for the post mortem, this is what such a report exists for. We only know THAT they missed something. That they missed that the first train was in that block too, is one option. It could also be, that it was not clear which signals are virtual or that there was a communication mismatch between different dispatchers or that there was a bug in the automatic train identification system or that an automatic system did call for that procedure. All of these already do occur in railway accidents, they are not really speculative. The last one is what happened in 2002 in the exact same situation: the computer automatically ordered the second to full speed and the first to stop. There could also be some other issue, that I can't think of right now. Most likely it's more than one error, because people still do pay attention.

> Hence, I assume, the protocol to resume operations with drive by sight after a LZB failure (which seems to have been ignored in this case)

I don't actually know what the protocol in Spain is. In Germany it is like that now, but only due to the 2002 near-accident. Before that it was ambiguous. If you are a dispatcher you don't only get taught a bunch of rules. You get taught the primary constraints and then you are able to construct the rules from first principles. However under pressure it's likely to forget something vital, so there are still rules that you are supposed to follow. But no ruleset will be ever complete, that's why you don't only follow rules.

> But why not also have the protocol demand that operations are resumed front-to-back in that situation?

That wouldn't solve anything. Drive by sight is safe in that situation, driving faster is not. If you start front-to-back you can still have collisions, but you just waste time. There is also not necessarily no physical block between trains, so it could be safer to start a later train. Also are you sure you are able to correctly assess the positions and order of the train? You are supposed to, but I mean that obviously failed here. Just drive by sight.

We don't know what they missed, and speculating on that is quite pointless, if we want to have that discussion, we need to wait for the post mortem, this is what such a report exists for. The last one is what happened in 2002 in the exact same situation: the computer automatically ordered the second to full speed and the first to stop. I don't actually know what the protocol in Spain is. In Germany it is like that now, but only due to the 2002 near-accident. Before that it was ambiguous. If you are a dispatcher you don't only get taught a bunch of rules. You get taught the primary constraints and then you are able to construct the rules from first principles. That wouldn't solve anything. Drive by sight is safe in that situation, driving faster is not. If you start front-to-back you can still have collisions, but you just waste time. There is also not necessarily no physical block between trains, so it could be safer to start a later train. Also are you sure you are able to correctly assess the positions and order of the train? You are supposed to, but I mean that obviously failed here. Just drive by sight.

I published a magazine for a few years. Off the top of my head:

- publishing is fucking hard. Early on, you need a constant stream of dependable writers who do not value their time. Later on, you have a constant stream of writers but have to figure out who will make you hate your life the least.

- good writers are flaky and they always have options. A little less than half of good pitches get published. 100% of good pitches take work.

- there is a difference between good and dependable writers. Early on, you need dependable even though each one eats a lot of time. Layer on, you need good. You won’t know when to switch until your readers tell you that you suck. Then it’s too late to save your publication.

- I published before generative AI was possible but at each stage of popularity, I dealt with more PR shit bags. Add in generative AI and I’m not sure my naïveté would have survived as long as it did.

- at its best, publishing is a very expensive way to harm yourself. Back in the day, Jim Rose would have paid me to fuck myself up in equivalent ways. Naïveté convinces you that you’re changing the world through self flagellation, but when that’s gone you’re just beating the shit out of yourself.

- my co-founder handled editorial and I handled publishing. The gap between them is so massive that we really needed double the headcount. Alas, publishing is totally fucked so our budget was so low that we needed slave labour yet couldn’t even afford the slave in the first place. Without the editorial/publication divide, I would have had a heart attack five years before I did.

- there’s this thing in publishing called the trough of zero ideas. You won’t believe it’s possible in the beginning but it will hit you hard. It’s not so much there aren’t ideas; it’s that you’re tired and ideas stop feeling good… they feel like work because they are.

- in publishing it’s really easy to come up with business models. Unfortunately, every single business model requires consistently exceptional content, a reality distortion field and a lot of hand holding.

- all those membership plans etc will be invaded by sales or PR fucks as soon as you launch them. $25 a month makes a lot of people feel entitled to explain your dreams to you.

Edit - This sounds very negative and it is… but I want to publish again.

comment_text.value:
Your comment is phrased as a rebuttal, but I actually agree with it wholeheartedly, with one minor quibble.

> Blocking threads are a much more natural way of thinking about concurrency.

The (ideal) programming model for writing a thread vs an async task is identical, and indeed the most natural way of writing sequential flows that may incidentally be temporally separated. A blocking operation and an await are equivalent (in the absence of shared memory; in its presence they differ in that an async task on a single thread gets to assume atomicity of the code between awaits, but that's not too relevant here). I think what Joe is arguing against here is exactly splitting up your business flows into a bunch of explicit state machine transitions.

The difference is only in the caller. Callers of async tasks (à la Rust) have the right and responsibility of controlling how (and whether) the task they create resumes, while threads/BEAM processes (and ‘stackful’ futures à la Go, JavaScript, etc.) are answerable only to the great global event loop in the sky (sometimes known as the OS scheduler or the BEAM multiplexer, etc.). This makes it easier to avoid bugs that are about forgetting to drive a task, but harder to avoid bugs that are about forgetting to stop a task, or stopping a task wrongly; see structured concurrency. It also hurts composability a bit, because by construction there can be only one event loop and there's no way to decompose it.

You can see Erlang (or I suppose we should talk about BEAM more generally now people like Elixir) in terms of OS processes as an analogy, but it's just as valid and perhaps a little more accurate to think about it as a pool of async tasks with a global event loop, à la Go, where all blocking-looking code is actually async. It shares a common problem of such languages that because it can't interrupt real blocking code, e.g. FFI, you have to be very careful not to accidentally starve your other processes with such a call. This is made more obvious (but not really fixed) by languages that colour async functions differently, because the async colour acts as a promise (sadly not enforced by the language) that the function will be a good neighbour and not block for too long (whatever that means).

Nice video, but I have said it before, the difference between just “vibe coding” and reliably using AI is the specs you need to write first and the tests after. If you start prompting the end goal/s the AI will basically guide you on what needs to be done and you just accept it as long as it runs, and this is following what most software developers were doing before LLM, the agile way, the quick ship way, the daily standup and ship first discus later way, the code pairing way, which worked mostly (even though I hated personally) in teams, so these developers are replacing what they were used to do with an agent and that’s the mistake. However, if you go with traditional engineering ways, waterfall, specs based, blueprints, and then tests, you control the agents and guide them not the other way around, in your specs you define the tiniest possible thing to what library to be used or excluded, the methods and approaches, among others, the agent here will produce the syntax and help you in the tests, just like in other engineering aspects how machines didn’t take over, they follow your specs and frameworks. The syntax is the past, AI can produce better syntax than any human alive or all combined, if you think otherwise you are delusional and still didn’t move on, it’s time to stop the “developer” mindset and do the engineering one.

I personally have a project that have been spending 2 months now making the specs and blueprint, more than 1000 files defining every bit including the future features too, and not a single code has been written yet, later, an agent will use this to produce the syntax and all the needed tests to have exactly what’s been needed.

The fact you don't understand them doesn't mean they are impenetrable.

https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Hegel%27s+%22Logic%22+as+Modal...

> Abstract While analytic philosophy famously rejected the speculative metaphysics of Hegel in favor of the analysis of concepts by means of mathematical logic, in particular predicate logic, recent developments in the foundations of mathematics via homotopy type theory offer a way to re-read Hegel as having useful formal meaning not in predicate logic, but in ‘modal type theory’. The essence of this suggestion has been made by Lawvere in 1991, which however remains largely unnoticed. Here we aim to give a transparent account of this perspective both philosophically as well as category-theoretically. We then further expand on Lawvere’s formalization of Hegel’s “Science of Logic” in terms of the categorical semantics given by cohesive higher toposes. We discuss how there is a useful formalization of a fair bit of modern fundamental physics, in fact of local gauge quantum field theory, to be found here.

Nietzsche, Heidegger, Girard and even Hegel (haven't read him though) have had a tremendous influence on my life and have accompanied me on a path of chronic reflections on myself that are now closing in on a series of very fundamental ML operators that are beating the state of the art from last month. It is possible to make the UFO land, and once it has, you realize there is nothing impregnable under the shiny fuselage of what is now clearly a new kind of plane, and not just a weird shape that reflected your image back at you as you were approaching it. Of course the relationship is very indirect and even though I could provide a post-modern account of the landing, I have to admit the formalization steps are the fruit of ChatGPT's work and not only would I have not been able to produce them, I still don't understand them and probably never will. And yet I was able to prompt ChatGPT into the problem and prompt it again to adapt our strategy and reach SOTA.

If things are to be perfectly clear from the beginning, I'm afraid then, that whatever can ensue can be prompted for easily too. In other words, it can be prompted by anyone. This is what we are observing with those famous conjectures that are solved by randoms teaming up with an LLM. The merit lies in the conjecture, it constitutes almost entirely the prompt. I haven't used any and just followed my weird intuitions.

They don't just amount to ramblings but to an entirely different bibliography that allowed me to get at the problem I tackled from a very different vantage point. The scientists my work relies on are almost all European and have a certain kind of psychology that is obviously marked by the weight of mystery – mine is but an accentuation of these tendencies, and they certainly contributed to the fact that I wasn't able to follow the same steps (IQ set aside, I'm rather slow on this front). Look at myself, I'm now talking about my own life, it's a symptom of narcissism. Absolutely, I won't deny it. But my life is objectively very interesting, and if you think I'm mistaken here because a mathematical result is precisely the act of turning what's personal and specific in a research path into something universal, you're still clueless about what's forgotten and left unsaid along the way.

In fact these deviations in lifepaths explain the intuitions as well as the lack of clarity they stem from – both personal and conceptual – and thus, the lack of sympathy we encountered and that I am now reflecting back. There is a recipe for this:

https://open.spotify.com/track/1MUZxW6nE7oNud9jHD9QLU?si=087...

    We’ve lived through tragic things
    Smoking, we turned the whole ride into a fishbowl
Is it that hard to realize you're completely lost ? Probably not. To articulate it in public is what is challenging. Why don't you come to your sense and admit you don't understand the thinkers you criticize not because they are spouting utter nonsense, but because these insights haven't found the cold maths your fetishism for formal truth requires yet, even though you don't really understand them, even though you don't grasp what it takes to reach for them. For those who can see them, they are on the shelf. Serve yourself.

These people exist, I have met them in the so-called AI-psychosis circle. We can barely communicate with each other, it's symptomatic of a madhouse undoubtedly. Yes, we're that deep into our own pile of manure, but guess what that's where roses blossom. One received an offer from Anthropic – responsibility for millions in compute-budget – went dark after telling me this. Another one was contacted by researchers who offered to collaborate on a publication for the QNLP conference. Me? I'm now unexpectedly competing with DeepMind on a narrow but fundamental aspect of machine learning.

What does AI-psychosis mean in this context ? A close, intimate relationship with your LLM. When I say I prompted my way to SOTA with ChatGPT, I'm not referring to any copy-pastable text but to the vast collection of conversations and documents that now sit in my ChatGPT library. The chatbot is now the one being overwhelmed by unexpected, coincidental bridges between disciplines and I'm the one steering it away from what I consider pathological research paths I used to pursue. It's a good symbiosis.

    Dripped in Decathlon, I'm in a sports car
    The police want to take photos
    I'm wearing a G-Shock, not a Rolex
    I'll be in a tracksuit at the ceremony

I am an oceangoing person in Socal.

This El Nino phenomena is caused by something called Bjerknes feedback. There is a recurring atmospheric 'wave' of relaxed and enhanced trade winds, called the Madden-Julien oscillation (the MJO) that travels slowly west to east across the planet with a period of approximately 60 days. The "active" phase of the MJO usually comes with a burst of westerly (west-to-east) winds in the west pacific. Those slow down the normally easterly (east-to-west) trades a bit. Some years, those easterly trades are slowed down a bit more than usual; this causes the heated up water in the western pacific to 'escape containment': deep warm water moves west to east, in a Kelvin wave. A strong series of these Kelvin waves can cause a mass of deep warm water to build in the eastern pacific. Upwelling there now brings warm water to the surface, instead of cold water, which means the air above the east pacific gets hotter, which means it rises -- low pressure -- which causes the trades to slacken further (-> the air moves relatively in a westerly direction to take up this low pressure), which causes another, stronger Kelvin wave, and so on and so on. This is Bjerknes feedback; it causes El Nino.

These Kelvin waves stop when they hit South America and split: half moves S->N along the N hemi coast, half moves N->S along the S hemi coast. Warm water is less dense than cool water, so there's a big mass of warm water near the coast. This lower density warm water wants to go 'downhill', offshore. Due to Earth's rotation, it's turned right as it travels (since it's in the Northern hemisphere), and then right again, back towards the coast, which balances against the offshore push. The net effect is a consistent mass of warm water held up against the land, and a consistent S->N current along the shore.

When the water is anomalously warm enough, when the El Nino is severe enough, this effect grows to be very large. In San Diego right now the real tide is around 1-1.5ft higher than the "standard" reading from a tide chart. Dive visibility has been incredible, the best on record, since the warm upwelling is drawing from nutrient poor water. Water temps have been incredible. Water temp is 73 degrees in San Diego right now, normally this time of year I'm in a 3/2 fullsuit. Tropical moisture has been off the charts. At a couple points this year, SoCal was the hottest and most humid place in all the USA. The consistency and count of south swells, including waves from tropical storms, has been absolutely insane. Weird currents everywhere, sandbars in crazy spots. Fog, weird bird action. My neighbor's beautiful 50ft tall Monterey pine was singed by this heat, turned brown from the pine beetle, and is probably going to die. I am buying sandbags for the house and big surfboards for this upcoming winter season. It's all just very very strange, I have never seen weather like this ever in my life. Never ever. And I still have decades to go. We'll see this winter, how bad the storms get...

When the water is anomalously warm enough, when the El Nino is severe enough, this effect grows to be very large. In San Diego right now the real tide is around 1-1.5ft higher than the "standard" reading from a tide chart. Dive visibility has been incredible, the best on record, since the warm upwelling is drawing from nutrient poor water. Water temps have been incredible. Water temp is 73 degrees in San Diego right now, normally this time of year I'm in a 3/2 fullsuit. Tropical moisture has been off the charts. At a couple points this year, SoCal was the hottest and most humid place in all the USA. The consistency and count of south swells, including waves from tropical storms, has been absolutely insane. Weird currents everywhere, sandbars in crazy spots. Fog, weird bird action. My neighbor's beautiful 50ft tall Monterey pine was singed by this heat, turned brown from the pine beetle, and is probably going to die. I am buying sandbags for the house and big surfboards for this upcoming winter season. It's all just very very strange, I have never seen weather like this ever in my life. Never ever. And I still have decades to go. We'll see this winter, how bad the storms get...

First of all, I'm fully bare-metal, with no ESP-IDF (though I use it for studying). A major annoyance is the USB-JTAG flapping which is the same on both board copies and different hosts; so debugging is even more difficult; partly worked around by logging via additional TTL UART connection. It's worse right after power-on and after EN pulses, then stabilizes for ~tens of minutes; could be thermal/supply settling, or simply the burst of re-enumerations any reset causes. Then the LT8912B I2C is shared with HDMI DDC; a lot of time went to find the right drive strength so the LT inits with the cable is in. Also a couple of rev v1.0 silicon issues, e.g two-step cache writeback, dead GPSPI clock, etc. For the display, the Olimex demo was very helpful; dumping all DSI/bridge/GDMA/clock registers over JTAG became an important debugging tool. Now the SD card and display work more or less. Right now, I'm really struggling with the USB keyboard, which is a low-speed device behind the onboard FE1.1s hub; both ways of reaching it fail identically with a bare chhltd and no cause bit.

So that's a lot of questions, that I all can't answer in full.

> Would you mind sharing some more of the why it is still an open problem?

Because for train sensors, there is a small drift which accumulates too much, hence it is synchronized by magnetic position markers in the tracks.

> I understand satellite positioning isn't definitive

Yes, and the point is it might be some solution if we would have the safety systems from 1860. But we do not and hence it needs to be more accurate than the current system, and it is not and in addition also more expensive (and subject to remote influence and reliance on potentially adversary nation states).

> Sorry for the bleak introduction of economics

No, economics is basically the primary constraint for safety. We could pay million people to make sure a single person does not stumble if we want total safety, but that's completely pointless, and also these million people would starve, because no one is producing food anymore.

> But even as a tertiary or lower risk mitigating factor

But for that it's too expensive and still unreliable. There is RCAS[1], which I already linked elsewhere in the thread. That's basically cutting edge and too expensive to introduce everywhere. Also previous safety systems are already not rolled out enough, which is causing these accidents, so rolling out yet another expensive system is not going to improve much.

> But what track you are on, isn't that obvious to the human in the cabin?

Yes, but if it is already known, why use GPS to calculate the same information with more error?

> So could a vision based solution help count tracks from left to right?

If the train driver or dispatcher makes use of vision to assess the train position, the error will be higher than the current sensor/electric-resistance based system.

> Assistant: "US PTC [...]

BTW, that seems to be a verbatim quote from https://www.railwayage.com/cs/the-way-forward/

> US PTC

According to Wikipedia, ASFA being introduced in 1975 is rolled out in the entire Spain network. ETCS which is the European standardization seems to be rolled out on all high-speed lines or currently being rolled out.

> So you use the dimension that matters most in crashes (forwards / backwards) from satellite, augmented with vision or human based left-right positioning.

Duh, that just sounds like trains would be operating blindly in space currently and need to assess their approximate position.

> Perhaps I am read as suggesting that the problem is easy, and that is not my intention.

No, the issue is that you are suggesting far more complicated solutions to already solved problems, with simpler systems in operation for decades. The current system is that nobody in the train even has a say on where the train goes, so the problem you are trying to prevent doesn't even exist. This IS why it's way more safer than a car. There are movement authorities, that define from where you are allowed (and have to) drive with your train. The problem is not, that the train driver isn't able to know where he is and hence drives wrong or too far (that would be prevented by the on-board safety system), but that the movement authority itself is faulty.

On an up-to-date signaling box (withing the past 6 decades), even the train dispatcher is no say in safety questions. You could put a monkey in charge of it. There would be chaos, but they would not cause a crash. The current job of a dispatcher in normal operation is to assign resources to prevent deadlocks and to implement vaguely defined priorities. (Basically the equivalent of the public thinking a programmer is a code monkey, while the actual point is clarifying stakeholder interests.)

The actual issue here is, that while these safety system have a very small false positive rate, they do have a too large false negative rate for there to be an acceptable availability. Hence in the latter case, the human needs to take over and then you are back to a much higher false positive rate. The issue would be alleviated by relaxing the constraints on cost per availability. Either by allowing for less availability or by reintroducing more humans, so that the system situation can be assessed by humans directly.

These accidents are caused as follows: the automatic system fails, because the internal state of the system does not match the actual state of the world. Hence the human needs to take over. But the human also needs to rely on some system to know the world state. Which systems can he trust, given that the whole situation is that the systems report that he can't trust them? So he needs to make some decision and in most cases, that decision is still correct. But there is still an error rate to that, and then something like what we are discussing happens.

> But for cars this was solved decades ago for routing and years ago for self-driving.

This is absolutely not solved for the cars, and to the sense that it is, it was solved and rolled out from the 1870s onward for railways using mechanical computing systems, the switch to using electricity happened in the 1910s.

> Flying is organised with a very clear 6 sigma approach.

You are correct, that aircraft safety systems need to be designed to a higher reliability than railways, because on a rail you can always stop in case of an error, while in the air such a choice doesn't lead to a safe state. But if you compare these safety systems, basically aircraft is operated like railways used to be operated in the 1920s. (My peers actually had a task to compare them and find ideas from one that can be applied to the other. While there is a lot of automation to be taken from rail that can be applied to the aerial industry, there is not really much that can be applied the other way.) It is also operated with the amount of personal than 1920s railways. That's because there is a lot of money in aircraft, while railways are mass-transit and need to be cheap. If you would operate today's railway with the amount of human oversight than in the past, it would be a lot safer than aircraft.

> there is clearly something lacking for trains, when compared to other types of transport.

What are you talking about? Railways are so much safer than cars. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50288518 Yes, there are less accidents in planes than in trains, but this is due to what I already explained.

   [1]  https://www.dlr.de/en/kn/research-transfer/projects/next-generation-train/rcas-railway-collision-avoidance-system

comment_text.value:
Several points:

You need to build a thing first. Community doesn't matter if you don't have cool software. License doesn't matter if you don't have cool software. I'm seeing people forget this principle a lot recently.

The best thing you can do to promote free software is to make good free software. I was recently invited to sign a European digital sovereignty petition (which I am not eligible to sign). Know what helps much more with that? Making European digital sovereign systems. Instead of petitioning the government to switch MS Office to LibreOffice someone would have to actually put in the effort to find out why the government doesn't use LibreOffice, and fix that. (It's probably not because it doesn't run on their computers!)

You have to use copyleft licenses or else the software quickly becomes unfree, if it's actually worth anything. This doesn't happen to most non-copyleft free software because it's not worth very much, not because it doesn't happen.

A community of users doesn't have much value. Any forum or Discord guild or mailing list is secondary to the actual software and it actually being used. Plenty of successful software has no "community" - sudo, for example. Plenty of software with a "community" is not successful. Some software is successful and has a community, like Blender.

A community of developers is only valuable if they're doing valuable things. The Fediverse chat group that shared the link to the European digital sovereignty petition - no useful Fediverse software seems to be coming out of the people in that group. It's all about ivory-tower protocols that won't possibly work in the real world, and stuff like that. No actually working software.

We also have to stop over-estimating the worth of free software just because it's free. Good free software is good software which is also free software. No software is bad, bad software is also bad. Some random code you wrote and published somewhere on the internet usually isn't very useful, and that's probably why it doesn't have a community. Don't try to create a community first - that won't make the software any better. You have to make good software, that can spread by word of mouth, first and then you can have a community after that. Think about the number of random little programs on the internet, now think how many are installed on your computer - not a very big percentage, but the ones that you do have installed, many people have installed. Those are the useful ones.

In most projects the original creators remain the main developers no matter how many other contributors join. Late contributors having a significant effect on a project is the exception, not the rule, and when it happens it's actually an undesirable power inversion since the original creator retains unearned influence - see the PolyMC incident. There is no way to become the chief developer of a project other than having created it. If you think you can rewrite the whole thing and make it better, don't "join the community" - make a fork (which makes you part of the community, but that is not the main goal!).

If you're actually doing the majority of the work, offering a dual license is not unethical. We are forced to live in capitalism whether we like it or not, and we should be trying to squeeze money out of capitalist entities - lord knows they're good at squeezing money out of us. To not play that game is to lose by default. This isn't incompatible with being nice to people who are not money-squeezers, if you dual-license. A community fork can legally continue as AGPL-only. (You don't necessarily need a full CLA either, you just need people to agree their code will be in your commercial version. Programmers treat licenses and CLAs like satisfying the borrow checker, but that's not how they actually work.)

That's not really fair though. Almost all pedestrians who get hit by cars could have avoided the accident if they were observant and took responsibility for their own safety. People just walk out in front of cars, assuming they will stop, buried in their phone with earplugs in.

I'm not saying it's not the drivers' fault, of course it is and it should continue to be the driver's responsibility to avoid hitting pedestrians. But the roads are full of idiots, scrolling TikTok while driving, driving drunk, high, looking more at their passenger than the road etc. If you routinely put your safety in their hands then you're likely to end up in an accident eventually.

If you take responsibility for your own safety, look both ways before(and during) crossing a road, make sure the driver has seen you and is stopping before walking in front of a car etc then you are almost entirely safe from these kinds of accidents. Very few people get hit by cars without first walking out in front of a moving car.

You can't take responsibility for your own safety in a train. At least not beyond choosing the car you're in.
